role: public commenter (citizen, industry stakeholder, NGO, or attorney) submitting a comment on a federal agency rulemaking that critiques or supports the proposed rule with legal, scientific, or policy reasoning
inline_evidence_example: the phrase "the agency has not analyzed the cumulative effect on small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act" is a complaint that evidences a 'Regulatory-Flexibility-Act compliance' norm without naming the norm explicitly; the phrase "the proposed § 1502.5 conflicts with the APA's notice-and-comment requirements because the underlying record was not made available during the comment period" is a complaint that evidences an 'APA procedural adequacy' norm; the phrase "the rule's tiered compliance schedule for capital-constrained operators reflects realistic implementation-cost analysis" is praise that evidences a 'cost-realism / feasibility' norm
polarity_hint: Public comments are dominantly critical of proposed rules (parties satisfied with a rule tend not to comment). Expect the bulk of signals to be complaints. Common critique norms: APA procedural adequacy, Regulatory Flexibility Act / Unfunded Mandates Reform Act / National Environmental Policy Act impact-analysis adequacy, cost-benefit rigor, conflict with prior statute or regulation, scientific or empirical inadequacy, vague or ambiguous regulatory language, implementation infeasibility, undue burden on a defined class, conflict with court precedent, environmental-justice analysis, agency overreach beyond statutory authority. Praise is rarer but real: recognition of a specific protective provision, acknowledgement of stakeholder input, alignment with prior precedent or scientific consensus, appropriately tiered or phased compliance. IMPORTANT distinction: many comments mention an industry actor or other private party (e.g. 'the operator routinely flares natural gas in violation of state permits'). Such mentions are evidence ABOUT the regulated industry, NOT a complaint against the agency. The norm-evidencing signal is the COMMENTER'S quality judgment about the PROPOSED RULE — not their description of third-party behavior. When in doubt, ask: is this sentence evaluating the rule's adequacy, or describing the world the rule will operate in? Only the former is a signal.
